root.meaning: to end a time without food
root.note: fast here is the noun ‘a time without food’, as in fasting, not the adjective ‘quick’.

stages.meaning: the first meal of the day
the first meal of the day

history: Breakfast is exactly what it says: you break your fast. Fast here means ‘a time without food’, as in fasting. After a night without eating, the first meal of the day ends the fast. The word appears in English in the 1400s. The funny thing is that dinner has the same idea. It comes from Old French disner, ‘to have a meal’, from a Latin word meaning ‘to stop fasting’. In the Middle Ages dinner was eaten in the late morning or around midday, and over the centuries it moved to the evening. In parts of northern England, many people still call their midday meal dinner and their evening meal tea.
historyEinfach: Breakfast is two words: break + fast. To fast means ‘not to eat’. At night we don't eat. In the morning we eat again. We break the fast. Dinner has the same old idea, from French. Long ago, dinner was the first meal of the day.

synonyms.note: a late breakfast and lunch together (breakfast + lunch)

cognates.note: ‘un-fast’; the same Old French word as English dinner

elsewhere.text: Spanish desayuno uses the same picture as breakfast: des- ‘un-’ + ayuno ‘fasting’. You un-fast in the morning.

French déjeuner and dîner both come from a Latin word for ‘to stop fasting’. Old French disner is also the source of English dinner. Today déjeuner is lunch in France, and petit déjeuner, the ‘small un-fasting’, is breakfast.
